title: Introducing Yourself to Patients
notes: In the isiXhosa culture, it is expected that when one greets, he/she must greet with titles to assure politeness.

phrases.english: Miss / Ms (use if unsure of patient’s marital status)

bhuti (a respectful reference to an older male)

title: General Basic Health Enquiry
notes: In the isiXhosa culture, it is expected to ask ‘’How are you?’’ before proceeding with the conversation, whether you know that person or not. If you do not ask about ‘’ímpilo’’, you are regarded as impolite.
*Nosipho is a female name because it begins with ‘No-’’which indicates female

phrases.english: How are you feeling? (when someone is not well)
How is it? (ku-it is) = it is how?
I-speak a little bit of isiXhosa.
I beg your pardon. / Sorry, can-you-repeat.

title: Asking a Person’s Name and Surname
isiXhosa Clan Names
notes: A clan name is considered more important than a surname in isiXhosa communities. Asking for or addressing someone with a clan name is considered a sign of respect and politeness which makes the person feel good. The children take the father’s clan name. People in isiXhosa culture do not marry the same clan as it is considered incest in the isiXhosa community.

You will notice that the females have ‘Ma’ in front of their clan names which represent the female gender. When a daughter gets married, she will keep her clan name, but her children will not use her clan name but will use the husband’s clan name. With males, the children take the father’s clan name. As it is with individual names, so it is with clan names, girls names have ‘No’ to represent a female name as shown in the examples below:
